evidence: Cic. N.D. 2.99: bēstiārum vel cicurum vel ferārum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Opposed to cicur, tame. Of land it is untilled, and of people savage, fierce, cruel (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: a wild animal, a wild beast
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.50: neque ūllā rē longius absumus ā nātūrā ferārum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The adjective used as a noun (bēstia understood): the usual word for a wild animal, and also for game as food (Tac. Germ. 23.1, under wild, of plants).

phrases.latin: in bēstiīs, volucribus, nantibus, agrestibus, cicuribus, ferīs
phrases.english: in animals: birds, creatures that swim, beasts of the field, tame and wild

phrases.latin: calumniārī sī quis autem voluerit, quod arborēs loquantur, nōn tantum ferae, fictīs jocārī nōs meminerit fābulīs
phrases.english: and if anyone wants to carp because trees talk, not only wild beasts, let him remember that we are joking in made-up stories

sources: Lewis & Short: ferus · Lewis & Short: cicur
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 407.

Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica, loci-phaedrus), checked against the editions named there. Cicero’s De natura deorum and De officiis as Lewis & Short quotes them.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
